summary: A Hebrew adjective comes AFTER its noun and agrees with it in three things: gender, number and definiteness. Every adjective has four forms — masculine and feminine, singular and plural: גָּדוֹל, גְּדוֹלָה, גְּדוֹלִים, גְּדוֹלוֹת “big”. The endings are those of the nouns (-ָה or -ֶת or -ִית for the feminine, -ִים and -וֹת for the plural), and what counts is the noun’s grammatical gender, not its ending: שֻׁלְחָנוֹת גְּדוֹלִים “big tables” (a masculine noun with -וֹת), עִיר יָפָה “a beautiful city” (a feminine noun without -ָה). The article decides between a phrase and a sentence. Attributive — “the big house” — repeats the article on the adjective: הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל. Predicative — “the house is big” — leaves the adjective bare, and, as in every Hebrew present-tense sentence, there is no verb “to be”: הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל. So one ה turns a sentence into a phrase. In the past and the future the verb הָיָה appears (הַבַּיִת הָיָה גָּדוֹל). Often the first vowel shortens in the longer forms (גָּדוֹל → גְּדוֹלָה, יָקָר → יְקָרָה); short adjectives double their last letter (קַל → קַלָּה, קָטָן → קְטַנָּה). Feelings of heat and cold, and easy and hard, are said impersonally with לְ: חַם לִי “I’m hot”, קַר לָהּ “she is cold”, קָשֶׁה לִי “it is hard for me” — the adjective stays masculine singular. There are no cases, so nothing else changes.

blocks.caption: Four forms; the endings are the noun endings -ָה / -ֶת / -ִית, -ִים, -וֹת. Adjectives in -ֶה turn it into -ָה; ־ִי takes ־ִית.

items.title: Attributive: “the big house” (a phrase)
points: הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל — the big house: the article on both words
בַּבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל — in the big house: the adjective keeps its הַ

items.title: Predicative: “the house is big” (a sentence)
points: הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל — the house is big: no article on the adjective, no verb
הַבַּיִת לֹא גָּדוֹל — the house is not big
הַבַּיִת הָיָה גָּדוֹל — the house was big

blocks.title: One ה makes the difference
blocks.text: הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל = “the big house” (a phrase, waiting for a verb). הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל = “the house is big” (a complete sentence). Read the article on the adjective before you translate.

head: the article before the adjective
example
rows: הֶ before an unstressed חָ or עָ
blocks.caption: The same rules as for nouns (lesson 4).

head: pattern
masculine → feminine
examples
rows: יָקָר → יְקָרָה, צָעִיר → צְעִירָה, עָצוּב → עֲצוּבָה, זָקֵן → זְקֵנָה
קַל → קַלָּה, חַם → חַמָּה, קָטָן → קְטַנָּה
blocks.caption: You do not have to predict the forms: learn each adjective with its feminine — the drills ask for exactly that.

head: impersonal (with לְ)
meaning
rows: it is hard for me to get up
blocks.caption: The adjective stays masculine singular; the person is in לְ: never *אֲנִי חַם for “I’m hot”.

blocks.title: The noun’s gender, not its ending
blocks.text: שֻׁלְחָנוֹת גְּדוֹלִים (m., although -וֹת), נָשִׁים יָפוֹת (f., although -ִים), עִיר יָפָה (f., no ending), עֵינַיִם כְּחֻלּוֹת (f.). Check the gender of the noun in its word card.

blocks.title: Several adjectives
blocks.text: They follow one another, each agreeing: בַּיִת גָּדוֹל וְיָפֶה “a big and beautiful house”, הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל וְהַיָּפֶה. “Very” (מְאוֹד) comes after the adjective: יָפֶה מְאוֹד.

blocks.title: With a possessive
blocks.text: שֶׁלִּי can stand after the adjective or between: הַבַּיִת הֶחָדָשׁ שֶׁלִּי = הַבַּיִת שֶׁלִּי הֶחָדָשׁ “my new house” — the adjective keeps its article.

blocks.title: Ask yourself before you write an adjective
questions: Is it a phrase (“the big …”) or a sentence (“… is big”)?
What is the gender of the noun — and is it singular or plural?
Is the noun definite (הַ, a name, שֶׁל…)? Then the adjective takes הַ too.

askYourself: Where does the adjective go? → after the noun: בַּיִת גָּדוֹל.
Masculine or feminine noun (its gender, not its ending)? → גָּדוֹל or גְּדוֹלָה.
Is the noun definite? → in a phrase the adjective takes the article too: הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל.
Is it a statement “X is Y”? → no article on the adjective and no verb in the present: הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל.
A feeling (hot, cold, easy, hard) of a person? → adjective + לְ: חַם לִי.
steps: Find the noun and its gender and number.
Choose the form of the adjective.
Decide phrase or sentence: article on the adjective only in the phrase.

traps: *הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל for “the big house” — that is “the house is big”; the phrase is הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל.
*בַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל — the article goes on both words or on none.
יָשָׁן is “old” for things; for people זָקֵן or, politely, מְבֻגָּר.
יָפֶה (m.) and יָפָה (f.) are written the same way; so are קָשֶׁה / קָשָׁה and כֵּהֶה / כֵּהָה.

quiz.why: In a phrase the adjective repeats the article. הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל is a sentence: “the house is big”.
No article on the adjective = a sentence; Hebrew has no verb “to be” in the present.
The adjective follows the noun and takes its gender — עִיר is feminine although it has no -ָה.
שֻׁלְחָן is masculine; the -וֹת of its plural does not make it feminine.
Feeling hot or cold is impersonal: the adjective + לְ.
Before an unstressed חָ the article is הֶ: הֶחָדָשׁ (but הַחֲדָשָׁה).
יָשָׁן is for things; for people זָקֵן, or politely מְבֻגָּר.
Adjectives in ־ִי take ־ִית in the feminine.

seeAlso.note: Arabic is Hebrew’s twin here: the adjective follows the noun and copies its gender, number and definiteness (الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ “the big house”, الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ “the house is big”) — and also its case; non-human plurals take a feminine singular adjective.

German puts the adjective before the noun and gives it an ending only there (das große Haus, ein großes Haus); after sein it never changes (das Haus ist groß) — Hebrew changes it in both places, but only for gender and number.
Chinese adjectives are verbs: 房子很大 “the house is big” needs no 是, as Hebrew needs no verb “to be”; before a noun they take 的 (很大的房子) and never change.

notes.text:
Greek adjectives come before the noun (το μεγάλο σπίτι); Hebrew ones follow it and repeat the article:
→ הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל

Agreement in gender and number works as in Greek, without the neuter and without cases.

Russian adjectives come first and agree in case too (большой дом, в большом доме); Hebrew ones follow the noun, never change for case, but take the article:
→ הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל

As in Spanish, the adjective usually follows and agrees in gender and number:
→ casa grande ~ דִּירָה גְּדוֹלָה

New is that it repeats the article — without it the phrase becomes a sentence:
→ הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל “the big house”
→ הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל “the house is big”

English adjectives come first and never change; Hebrew ones follow the noun, have four forms and repeat the article.

“The big house” and “the house is big” differ by one ה:
→ הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל / הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל

As in French, most adjectives follow and agree (une maison blanche ~ דִּירָה לְבָנָה); Hebrew also repeats the article:
→ הַדִּירָה הַלְּבָנָה
German adjectives come first and change with the article and the case (der große Tisch, ein großer Tisch); Hebrew ones follow the noun, take הַ when the noun has it, and have only four forms.

Hindi adjectives come first, and those in -ā agree (बड़ा घर, बड़ी गाड़ी); Hebrew adjectives follow the noun, all of them agree, and they take the article:
→ הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל

Persian also puts the adjective after the noun, joined by ezafe (خانهٔ بزرگ ~ בַּיִת גָּדוֹל); but Persian adjectives never change, while Hebrew ones agree in gender and number and repeat the article.

Marathi adjectives come first, and some agree (मोठा मुलगा / मोठी मुलगी); Hebrew adjectives follow the noun and all agree:
→ יֶלֶד גָּדוֹל / יַלְדָּה גְּדוֹלָה

The same rule as Arabic: the adjective follows and agrees in gender, number and definiteness (الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ ~ הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל; الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ ~ הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל).

Hebrew has no case, and plural things take plural adjectives.

Turkish adjectives come first and never change (büyük ev, büyük evler); Hebrew ones follow the noun and agree:
→ בַּיִת גָּדוֹל, בָּתִּים גְּדוֹלִים

Japanese い-adjectives behave like verbs and can end a sentence (家は大きい); Hebrew adjectives are not verbs — they follow the noun and agree, and the present needs no verb:
→ הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל

Korean adjectives are verbs (집이 커요); Hebrew adjectives agree like nouns, and a present sentence has no verb at all:
→ הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל
Finnish adjectives come first and copy the noun’s case and number (isossa talossa); Hebrew ones follow, copy gender, number and the article, and never take a case.

Hungarian adjectives come first and do not agree (nagy házak); Hebrew adjectives follow the noun and agree:
→ בָּתִּים גְּדוֹלִים

As in Swahili, the adjective follows the noun and agrees with it (kitabu kikubwa, vitabu vikubwa); Hebrew agrees in gender and number and adds the article:
→ הַסֵּפֶר הַגָּדוֹל
As in Luganda, the adjective follows the noun and agrees with it (omuntu omulungi “a good person”); Hebrew agrees in gender, number and definiteness.

Chinese adjectives come first (大房子) and work like verbs in a sentence (房子很大); Hebrew adjectives follow the noun and agree, and the sentence needs no 很 or 是:
→ הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל
As in Vietnamese, the adjective follows the noun (nhà lớn ~ בַּיִת גָּדוֹל); but Hebrew adjectives change for gender and number and take the article.

Inuktitut often says “big” or “small” with a suffix inside the noun (iglujuaq “a big house”); Hebrew uses a separate adjective after the noun:
→ בַּיִת גָּדוֹל

As in Italian, the adjective usually follows the noun and agrees in gender and number (la casa grande, le case grandi ~ דִּירָה גְּדוֹלָה, דִּירוֹת גְּדוֹלוֹת).

New is the second article: הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל “the big house” — without it the phrase becomes a sentence, הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל “the house is big”.

As in Portuguese (a casa grande, as casas grandes), the adjective follows the noun and agrees in gender and number.

Hebrew also repeats the article on it — הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל “a casa grande” — and leaves it off to make a sentence:
→ הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל “a casa é grande”

Like Albanian, Hebrew puts the adjective after the noun and makes it agree (djalë i mirë, vajzë e mirë ~ יֶלֶד טוֹב, יַלְדָּה טוֹבָה).

Where Albanian adds the linking article i / e, Hebrew repeats the definite article: djali i mirë ~ הַיֶּלֶד הַטּוֹב.

If your adjectives have endings that carry gender, number and case at once, Hebrew is simpler: four forms (גָּדוֹל, גְּדוֹלָה, גְּדוֹלִים, גְּדוֹלוֹת) and no case.

What is new is the place — after the noun — and the repeated article:
→ הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל

If adjectives in your language stand before the noun and never change, two habits are new: the Hebrew adjective follows the noun, and it copies the noun’s gender, number and article (הַדִּירָה הַגְּדוֹלָה).

One ending (־ָה, ־ִים, ־וֹת) carries gender and number together.

If adjectives in your language work like verbs and need no “to be”, the Hebrew present feels familiar:
→ הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל “the house (is) big”

New: the adjective changes for gender and number, and the article decides between a phrase (הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל) and a sentence.

If your language expresses qualities with verbs or affixes inside one long word, treat the Hebrew adjective as a separate word after the noun that copies its gender, number and article:
→ הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל, הַדִּירָה הַגְּדוֹלָה

In many Semitic languages the adjective follows the noun and agrees with it in gender, number and definiteness; Hebrew does exactly this (הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל), with no case.

If your language puts the adjective first, reverse the order in Hebrew.
